title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 173
paragraphs: Now the Carians were reduced to subjection by Harpagos without any brilliant deed displayed either by the Carians themselves or by those of the Hellenes who dwell in this land. Among these last are, besides others, the men of Cnidos, settlers from Lacedemon, whose land runs out into the sea, being in fact the region called Triopion, beginning from the peninsula of Bybassos. Since all the land of Cnidos except a small part is washed by the sea (for the part looking toward the North is bounded by the Gulf of Keramos, and that looking to the South by the sea off Syme and Rhodes), the men of Cnidos began to dig through this small part, which is about five furlongs across, while Harpagos was subduing Ionia, desiring to make their land an island. Within the isthmus, all was theirs; for where the territory of Cnidos ends in the direction of the mainland, there is the isthmus which they were digging across. While the Cnidians were working at it with a great number of men, it was observed that the men who worked suffered injury much more than might have been expected, and in a more supernatural manner — both in other parts of their bodies and especially in their eyes, when the rock was being broken up. So they sent men to ask the Oracle at Delphi what the cause of the difficulty was. And the Pythian prophetess, as the men of Cnidos themselves report, gave them this reply in trimeter verse:
“Fence not the place with towers, nor dig the isthmus through; for Zeus would have made your land an island, had he willed it so.”

When the Pythian prophetess had given this oracle, the men of Cnidos not only ceased from their digging, but when Harpagos came against them with his army, they delivered themselves to him without resistance.
